1. Whether summary judgment was properly granted on plaintiff's claim of defamation.
2. Whether summary judgment was properly granted on plaintiff's claim of intentional infliction of emotional distress.
3. Whether summary judgment was properly granted on plaintiff's claim that the defendants interfered with his contractual relations with another.
4. Whether summary judgment was properly granted with respect to plaintiff's claims for breach of lease.
5. Whether summary judgment was properly granted on plaintiff's claim for breach of quiet enjoyment of the premises.

II. STATEMENT OF THE CASE
Plaintiff-Appellant's complaint was filed on August 29, 2007, and contained five counts against Defendant-Appellees RCP Mayfield, LLC. (hereinafter "Mayfield") and Carey Young (hereinafter "Young"). All counts concern Plaintiff-Appellants' tenancy at the Village at Mayfield apartment complex which is owned and now operated by Mayfield and where Young is the property manager.
The first count in the complaint was a defamation claim against Young. The second count alleged intentional infliction of emotional distress by Young. The third count claimed that Young interfered with Plaintiff-Appellant's contractual relations with another apartment complex. The fourth count was a breach of lease claim against Mayfield surrounding provisions of the leases concerning utility payments by Mayfield and its tenants. The final count claimed deprivation of quiet enjoyment of the premises due to the breaches of the leases by Mayfield and Young.
The remaining dates concerning the filing of pleadings and motions in the trial court listed by Plaintiff-Appellant in his brief are accurate.
III. STATEMENT OF THE FACTS
A. Plaintiff-Appellant's Tenancy at Village of Mayfield
1. Plaintiff-Appellant Moves In
Plaintiff-Appellant moved into the Village at Mayfield apartment complex on June 5, 1998. (See Depo. of Plaintiff, pp. 31-32). He moved into Unit #201 which was the only suite he occupied during his entire tenancy. (See Depo. of Plaintiff, p. 32). He
1

subsequently entered into several leases with the Village of Mayfield for various periods of time for the term of the lease, and moved out in April of 2007. (See Depo. of Plaintiff, pp. 37, 47, 49, 53-54, 58-59, 60-61, 65, 67).
2. Terms of Plaintiff-Appellant's Leases
When Plaintiff-Appellant initially moved into the Village of Mayfield, the initial lease, which was marked as Exhibit 1 to his deposition, provided that the resident agreed to arrange and pay for electricity or gas (applies) to the proper utility company from the date of move in. (See Depo. of Plaintiff, pp. 34-35). The language subsequently was changed in later leases to indicate that the landlord shall furnish and pay for the following utilities: electricity, gas, water/waste water, trash removal and cable. (See Depo. of Plaintiff, pp. 38- 40). Next to each of these utilities was a box to be checked. (See Depo. of Plaintiff pp. 38- 39). The lease language also provided that the landlord may modify the method by which utilities are furnished to the premises and/or billed to the resident during the term of the lease, including, but not limited to billing the resident for any utilities previously included within the rent provided that the utility addendum has been executed. (See Depo. of Plaintiff, p. 40). This utility payment language in the lease remained until the language changed for the lease term commencing April 1, 2005 and ending March 31, 2006. (See Depo. of Plaintiff, pp. 67-68). .
The April 1, 2005 through March 31, 2006 lease, which was marked as Exhibit 10 of plaintiff's deposition, provided that the resident's rent does not include a charge for utilities. (See Depo. of Plaintiff, p. 64). A utility addendum allocation was made part of this lease and provided that the resident agreed that the resident may, upon thirty days prior
2

written notice from the landlord to resident, begin receiving a bill for additional utilities and services. (See Depo. of Plaintiff, pp. 67-68). Accordingly, on November 1, 2005, the Village of Mayfield apartments properly notified the residents that they would commence billing for natural gas to the residents effective December 1, 2005. (See Exhibit 9 of Depo. of Plaintiff).
3. Complaints About Plaintiff-Appellant
a. Residents' Complaints
The staff at the Village of Mayfield, including, but not limited to, Heather Battaglia ("Battaglia") and Young received complaints from residents about the Plaintiff-Appellant looking in windows other apartments, antagonizing dogs so that they barked, and leaving unwanted notes under doors of residents. (See Affidavit of Heather Battaglia, 16). Other residents complained to Young of being harassed and stalked by Plaintiff-Appellant. (See Depo. of Young at p. 45). In fact, Young had to threaten to call the police on Plaintiff- Appellant if he did not stop harassing the other residents. (See Depo. of Young at p. 45).
Scott Genberg, a resident at the Village of Mayfield, complained about Plaintiff- Appellant to management. (See Depo. of Genberg at pp. 9-12). Mr. Genberg became aware that while he was at work one evening the police came to his apartment concerning complaints about his dogs' barking. (See Depo. of Genberg at p. 9). Mr. Genberg felt that the dogs were antagonized by persons sitting the chair outside of Mr. Genberg's bedroom window and Mr. Genberg felt that Plaintiff-Appellant had been in that chair antagonizing the dogs and had called the police improperly. (See Depo. Genberg at pp. 9-11). Mr. Genberg made complaints about Plaintiff-Appellant to Battaglia. (See Depo. Genberg at pp. 18-19).
3

Claudia Lanese, another tenant at the Village of Mayfield, complained about Plaintiff-Appellant's behavior towards her and her son. (See Depo. of Lanese at pp. 26- 28). In fact, one of the reasons Ms. Lanese moved out of the Village of Mayfield was because of dealing with Plaintiff-Appellant. (See Depo. of Lanese at p. 27). Specifically, Ms. Lanese was not happy with Plaintiff-Appellant leaving notes under her door. (See Depo. Lanese at pp. 18-19).
b. Staff's Complaints
Several staff members complained about having to deal with Plaintiff-Appellant because he wasted their time and monopolized them. (See Affidavit of Battaglia at "[ 5). Battaglia, in particular, had numerous problems in dealing with plaintiff and how he came to preoccupy her valuable work time. (See Affidavit of Battaglia at 11 7-8). Plaintiff- Appellant would visit Ms. Battaglia in the office and demand one hundred percent of her attention so that she could not even answer a telephone. (See Affidavit of Battaglia at { 8). On the other hand, Plaintiff-Appellant had no compunction about interrupting Battaglia when she was with another resident for trivial reasons. (See Affidavit of Battaglia at [ 8). Eventually, Plaintiff-Appellant's harassing behavior of Battaglia resulted in her requesting that he no longer have anything to do with her at work and that all of his contacts go through Young. (See Affidavit of Battaglia at 19). Young agreed to this plan and sent Plaintiff-Appellant an e-mail instructing him not to contact Battaglia and bother her any more. (See Affidavit of Battaglia, "[ 10 and Exhibit A thereto).
4. Plaintiff's Departure From The Village of Mayfield
On February 6, 2007, Plaintiff-Appellant sent notice of his intention to vacate his apartment on or about April 1, 2007. (See Depo. of Plaintiff at pp. 111-112, Exhibit 23 to
4

Deposition of Plaintiff). As a result, on February 20, 2007, Young e-mailed Plaintiff- Appellant confirming receipt of his notice to vacate and advising him that his suite had been re-rented for April 15, 2007 requiring Plaintiff-Appellant to move out no later than April 1 in order to have time to get the suite ready for the next tenants. (See Depo. of Plaintiff at pp. 113, Exhibit 24 to Deposition of Plaintiff). Despite his statements and his notice to vacate and Young's confirmation of the timetable, Plaintiff-Appellant refused to move out on April 1, 2007, instead he did not move out until April 9, 2007. (See Depo. of Plaintiff at pp. 119, 175).
B. Young's Contacts With Lakes of Aurora
Prior to moving out of the Village at Mayfield, Plaintiff-Appellant applied to rent an apartment at the Lakes of Aurora apartment complex. (See Depo. of Plaintiff at pp. 120-121). As part of the rental process at the Lakes of Aurora, the prospective tenants have to have their current landlord fill out a verification of residency form. (See Depo. of Ed Donnelly at p. 7; Depo. of Carol Kuchera at p. 8). On behalf of the Village at Mayfield, Young filled out the verification of residency form concerning Plaintiff-Appellant's tenancy at the Village at Mayfield. (See Depo. of Carey Young, pp. 76-82). Young indicated on this document that Plaintiff-Appellant was not leaving on good terms and she would not consider renting to the tenant in the future. (See Depo. of Young at pp. 79-80). She also stated on the form that Plaintiff-Appellant harassed staff and residents at the Village at Mayfield and did not agree with the terms of the leases after he signed them. (See Depo. of Young, p. 11).
Ed Donnelly, the Property Manager at the Lakes of Aurora, disapproved Plaintiff- Appellant's application because Plaintiff-Appellant was considered a difficult tenant who
5

had objected to dogs and had personal problems with the management. (See Depo. of Donnelly at pp. 8-9). Mr. Donnelly felt that Plaintiff-Appellant would not be a good fit for the Lakes of Aurora as a result. (See Depo. of Donnelly at pp. 9, 11).
IV. ARGUMENT OF LAW
Assignment of Error No. 1
THE TRIAL COURT PROPERLY GRANTED DEFENDANT-APPELLEE'S MOTION FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT.
The trial court properly granted Defendant-Appellee's motion for summary judgment because there were no issues as to any material fact and the Defendant-Appellees were entitled to judgment as a matter of law. Even in viewing the evidence and resolving any doubts in favor of the Plaintiff-Appellant, reasonable minds could decide all of the issues only in favor of the Defendant-Appellees. It is for those reasons that the trial court granted the summary judgment motion.
A. Standard of Review
The appellate court reviews a lower court's granting of summary judgment de novo. Brown v. Scioto Bd. of Comm'rs (1993), 87 Ohio App.3d 704. An appellate court reviewing the grant of summary judgment must follow the standards set forth in Civ. R. 56(C) "the reviewing court evaluates the record ... in the light most favorable to the non- moving party ... . The motion must be overruled if reasonable minds could find for the parties opposing the motion". Saunders v. McFaul (1990), 71 Ohio App.3d 46, 50.
6

B. Plaintiff-Appellant Has Not Established Any Defamation By Young. This court has held that a defamation claim consists of five elements:
1. A false statement of fact;
2. About the plaintiff;
3. Published to a third party;
4. With the required degree of fault by the defendant publisher; and,
5. Plaintiff was injured as a result of this statement.
Lynch v. Studebaker (Cuyahoga App. 2007), 2007-Ohio-4014 at | 29; Carabell v. Soto (Cuyahoga App. 2006), 2006-Ohio-3840 at 18.
Notably, truth is an absolute defense to a defamation action. Krems v. Univ. Hosp. of Cleveland (1999), 133 Ohio App.3d 6. Article I of the Ohio Constitution states that every citizen may freely speak, write and publish his sentiments on all subjects, being responsible for the abuse of the right; and no loss shall be passed to restrain or bridge the liberty of speech or of the press. Section 11. Article I, Ohio Constitution.
Statements of opinion are not defamatory as the first element in a defamation case requires the false statement of fact [emphasis added]. The Ohio Supreme Court has adopted a totality of the circumstances test to determine whether a statement is fact or opinion. Scott v. The News-Herald (1986), 25 Ohio St.3d 243, 250. Under this test, a court should consider the following four factors:
1. What is the specific language used?
2. Is the statement verifiable?
7

3. What is the general contacts of the statements?
4. What is the broader context in which this statement appeared?
Id.
In examining these four factors, the courts have fleshed them out. First, in reviewing a specific language, the Ohio Supreme Court focused on a how a reasonable reader would understand the statement. Vail v. Plain Dealer Publishing Co. (1995), 72 Ohio St.3d 279, 282. In doing so, the court examined the common usage or meaning of the allegedly defamatory words themselves in order to determine whether the statements at issue have a concise meaning that is likely to give rise to clear factual implications. Wampler v. Higgins (2001), 93 Ohio St.3d 111, 127-128. Statements that are "loosely definable" or "variously interpretable" cannot in most contexts support an action for defamation. Id. at 128.
The second factor of whether an allegedly defamatory statement is verifiable can be used to determine whether the statement at issue is objectively capable of proof or disproof. Id. at 129. A reader cannot rationally view and unverifiable statement as conveying actual facts. Ollman v. Evans (D.C. Cir. 1984), 750 F.2d 970-981. The third factor looks at the general context in which the statements appear while the last factor is the broader social context of the statement.
A defendant in a defamation action may also invoke the defense of "conditional" or "qualified privilege". A & B-Abell Elevator Co., Inc. v. Columbus/Central Ohio Bldg. & Constr. Trades Council (1995), 73 Ohio St.3d 1, 7. Where the circumstances of the
8

occasion for the alleged defamatory communications are not in dispute, the determination of whether the occasion gives the privilege is a question of law for the court. Id. No single statement or formula can sufficiently describe when publication of a defamatory matter should conditionally or qualifiably privileged, however, the best description is that a publication is privileged when it is fairly made by a person in the discharge of some public or private duty, whether legal or moral, or in the conduct of his own affairs, in matters where his interest is concerned. Id. at 8; Hahn v. Kotten (1975), 43 Ohio St.2d 237, 244.
The Hahn court explained further that a publication is conditionally or qualifiably privileged where circumstances exist, or are reasonably believed by the defendant to exist, which casts on him the duty of making a communication to a certain other person to whom he makes such communication in the performance of such duty, or whether the person is so situated that it becomes right in the interest of society that he should tell a third person certain facts, which he in good faith proceeds to do. Hahn, supra, at 245-246. The essential elements of a conditionally privileged communication may accordingly be enumerated as good faith and interest to be upheld, a statement limited in its scope to this purpose, a proper occasion and publication in a proper manner and to proper parties only. Id. The privilege arises from the necessity of full and unrestricted communication concerning the manner in which the parties have an interest or duty, and is not restricted within any narrow limits. Id. at 246.
The defense of a qualified privilege is deeply rooted in public policy. A & B-Abell Elevator Co., Inc., supra at 8. It applies in a variety of situations where society's interest in compensating a person for loss of reputation is outweighed by a competing interest that demands protection. Id. Accordingly, the privilege does not attach to the communication,
9

but to the occasion on which it is made and it does not change the actionable quality of the publication, but heightens the degree of fault. Id. at 8-9. This affords some latitude for error thereby promoting the free flow of information on an occasion worthy of protection. Jacobs v. Frank (1991), 60 Ohio St.3d 111, 114.
1. Plaintiff Cannot Establish The Prima Facie Elements of Defamation Based on Admissible Evidence In The Record.
As noted above, in order to make a prima facie case, Plaintiff-Appellant must produce admissible evidence that establishes each of the five elements of defamation. The primary problem with Plaintiff-Appellant's claims is that he cannot establish that Young made any false statements of fact about him. Initially, it must be emphasized that only admissible evidence in the record can be used in a summary judgment proceeding. Civ. R. 56(C) ("summary judgment shall be rendered forthwith if the pleadings, depositions, answers to interrogatories, written admissions, affidavits, transcripts of evidence, and written stipulations of fact, if any, timely filed in the action, show that there is no genuine issue as to any material fact and that the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. No evidence or stipulation may be considered except as stated in this rule.")
Clearly, only the forms of evidence referenced in Civ. Rule 56(C) can be used in determining a summary judgment. Indeed, the Defendant-Appellees moved to strike certain exhibits of the Plaintiff-Appellants that were contained in the opposition to the summary judgment motion. One of these was the handwritten notes of Penelope Meschewshi which were attached to the Memorandum in Opposition to the Summary Judgment Motion without any affidavit verifying their authenticity or laying the foundation
10

for there admissibility. Accordingly, they could not serve as a basis for opposing the summary judgment motion. Therefore, Plaintiff-Appellant's use of or reference to these notes in his brief is improper and cannot be considered by this Court as they are not admissible in this proceeding or in the trial court.
The statements of Young that are in the record were those contained on the "Verification of Residency Form" that Young filled out for the Lakes of Aurora. On that form, she indicated that Plaintiff-Appellant was not leaving on good terms nor would she consider to renting to him in the future because of harassment of other residents and staff, and that he would not agree with the terms of his leases after they were signed. (See Depo. of Young, Exhibit 11). As can be seen from the deposition testimony of Young and the Affidavit of Battaglia, there were complaints of harassment about the Plaintiff-Appellant from other residents and staff members. This evidence is uncontroverted in the record. This is not a false statement of fact, rather it is a true statement of fact and, as noted above, truth is an absolute defense in Ohio to defamation claims. It was also true that the Plaintiff-Appellant did not agree with the terms of his leases by virtue of his current claim that he was illegally charged for utility payments despite the clear language in the lease terms that the landlord could charge for additional utilities provided appropriate notice was given. In short, all of the statements made by Young on the Verification Residency Form were true and thus not defamatory.
Other statements referenced by Plaintiff-Appellant in his brief are statements by Young that are clearly opinion. The statement that Young would not renew Plaintiff- Appellant's lease is clearly a statement of opinion concerning her feelings about the Plaintiff-Appellant. It is not a statement of fact and thus cannot be defamatory. Moreover,
11

Young's assertion that the Plaintiff-Appellant was not leaving on good terms is again a statement of opinion concerning her feelings about the Plaintiff-Appellant and her dealings with him. This is not a statement of fact and thus cannot meet the prima facie elements of a defamation claim.
The statements referred to by Plaintiff-Appellant in his brief that are based on admissible evidence also fail to meet the prima facie requirements of a defamation claim. Plaintiff-Appellant claims that Young accused him of being a criminal by saying he was a stalker. However, the citation by Plaintiff-Appellant does not support this allegation and, in fact, completely contradicts his argument. Since Plaintiff-Appellant does not provide this Court with exact language, the defendants will:
Q. You said you had complaints and - strike that. What were the circumstances?
A. Complaints of other residents tired of being harassed by you.
Q. Harassed in what way?
A. Notes under the door. They felt they were being stalked by you.
Q. Stalked?
A. Mm-hmmm. Yes.
Q. What does stalked mean?
A. Watching everything they do.
(See Depo. of Young at p. 45).
This testimony demonstrates that Young was testifying what other residents felt when they related to her that they were being stalked by the Plaintiff-Appellant and that by
12

"stalked", she meant watching everything they do. This is not a criminal accusation and the context of the testimony reveals that no reasonable fact finder could conclude that Young was accusing the Plaintiff-Appellant of committing a criminal offense.
The alleged statements that Mayfield and Young would not renew Plaintiff- Appellant's lease and that Plaintiff-Appellant was not leaving the Village of Mayfield on good terms are clearly statements of opinion. They are not factual statements and, therefore, they cannot serve as the basis for a defamation claim.
The alleged statements that Plaintiff-Appellant would not agree with the terms of his lease after he signed it is not contradicted by Young checking "yes" as to whether the terms of lease were met by the tenant. Stating that the Plaintiff-Appellant would not agree with the terms is different from stating that Plaintiff-Appellant did not meet the terms. Therefore, Plaintiff-Appellant's evidence does not go to the point being made about Plaintiff-Appellant not agreeing with the terms of leases. Therefore, the evidence cited by Plaintiff-Appellant is irrelevant.
As for the alleged statements about Plaintiff-Appellant being afraid of dogs or harassing other tenants by taking notes of barking dogs, the evidence is clear that stating Plaintiff-Appellant had a fear of dogs is an opinion and the deposition testimony of Scott Genberg demonstrates that he complained about Plaintiff-Appellant to Mayfield personnel with respect to the dog barking issue.
With respect to the allegation that Plaintiff-Appellant harassed other residents and staff, the evidence from the Affidavit of Heather Battaglia demonstrates that residents and staff complained about Plaintiff-Appellant and there is no evidence to the contrary. The remaining statements identified by Plaintiff-Appellant in his brief as defamatory are not
13

supported by the evidence. The Affidavit of Heather Battaglia demonstrates the problems she had with the Plaintiff-Appellant and the deposition testimony of Claudia Lanese demonstrates that part of the reason she moved out of the Village of Mayfield was because of Plaintiff-Appellant.
In examining the Verification of Residency Form, it is clear that most of the statements found on there are opinion and not fact. In using the four factor test outlined by the Ohio Supreme Court in Scott v. The News Herald, supra, it is clear that these statements are opinions. In reviewing the specific language of the form, it should be noted that several of the allegedly defamatory statements cited by Plaintiff-Appellant were made by checking yes or no box. Answering yes or no is an opinion by Young and not a statement. The specific language used by Young was only yes or no and indicated agreement or disagreement with a statement. Therefore, the specific language factor certainly indicates that opinions were being stated and not facts. The second factor is whether the allegedly defamatory statement is verifiable. This factor is used to determine whether an allegedly defamatory statement is subjectively capable of proof or disproof. Wampler, supra at 129. In examining Young's alleged statements, there is no objective way to determine whether a tenant is leaving on good terms or not. This is clearly a subjective standard and, as such, cannot be defamatory.
The third factor looks at the general context in which the statements appear. In this case, the statements were made in a form that contained pre-printed questions. The boxes that were marked as "no" were both asking the person filling out the form to give their opinions on a prospective tenant. The general context clearly indicates that opinions were being requested of Young. The last factor is a broader social context of the statements.
14

There is nothing about the broader social context of these statements that leads one to conclude that they are defamatory or constitute statements of fact. Accordingly, these four factors clearly indicate that the statements made by Young on this form are opinions and not statements of fact. Therefore, they cannot be defamatory.
2. Young Was Conditionally or Qualifiably Privileged to Make the Alleged Defamatory Statements.
Young is entitled to this defense because the filling out of the Verification of Residency Form for the Lakes of Aurora was part of her private duty as the Property Manager for the Village of Mayfield. She had a duty to fill out this form just as other complexes fill out the form for people applying for residence at the Village of Mayfield. There is nothing on the Verification of Residency Form that indicated that Young was acting in bad faith. The essential elements of a condition of privileged communication are good faith, an interest to be upheld, a statement limited in scope to this purpose, proper occasion and a publication in a proper manner and to proper parties only. All of these elements have been met in this case.
Young filled out this form in good faith and had an interest in answering truthfully about a problem tenant to a future landlord. The statements that she made on this form were in response to the Lakes of Auroras contacting her unilaterally and she limited herself to answering only the questions asked by the Lakes of Aurora on its form. Furthermore, the publication of this form was made only to the Lakes of Aurora personnel who were the proper parties to whom the statements would be made and those statements were made in the proper manner. Accordingly, the conditional or qualified privilege attached to Young's
15
-

statements in the Verification of Residency Form because of the free flow of this information is worthy of protection in the rental apartment community. Therefore, the statements were not defamatory under the conditional or qualified privilege ..
C. Plaintiff-Appellant Has Not Proven Intentional Infliction of Emotional Distress
The Ohio Supreme Court, in the seminal case of Yeager v. Local Union 20 (1983), 6 Ohio St.3d, 369, 374, laid out the elements of a claim for intentional affliction of emotional distress as follows:
Intentionally or recklessly causing severe emotional distress through extreme and outrageous conduct. This cause of action requires that the emotional distress be severe unless it is accompanied by contemporaneous physical injury.
Binns v. Fredendall (1987), 32 Ohio St.2d 244.
Because the Plaintiff-Appellant has produced no admissible evidence that any contemporaneous physical injury resulted from any of the alleged intentional infliction of emotional distress by Young, Plaintiff-Appellant must set forth admissible evidence that demonstrates that any emotional distress was severe. The allegations made by the Plaintiff-Appellant on this issue do not meet that standard. Plaintiff-Appellant's claims of "sheer mean spiritedness", failure to replace unsanitary hallway carpet, not talking to co- tenants who allowed dogs to run loose, and her contacts with another apartment complex do not cause any reasonable person to exclaim, "outrageous!". Yeager, supra, at 374-375. It has also been held that the elements of an intentional infliction of emotional distress claim are that the Plaintiff-Appellant must show:
16

1. That the Defendant-Appellee either intended to cause emotional distress or knew or should have known that the actions taken would result in serious emotional distress;
2. That Defendant-Appellee's conduct was so extreme and outrageous as to go beyond all possible bounds of decency and was such that it would be considered utterly intolerable in a civilized community;
3. That Defendant-Appellee's actions were the proximate cause of Plaintiff-Appellant's psychic injury; and,
4. That the mental distress suffered by Plaintiff- Appellant is serious and of such nature that no reasonable person could be expected to endure it.
Pyle v. Pyle (1983), 11 Ohio App.3d 31, 34.
Liability for intentional infliction of emotional distress will only be found in the most extreme circumstances, that is, where the conduct has been so outrageous in character and so extreme in degree as to go beyond all possible bounds of decency and be regarded as atrocious, and utterly intolerable in a civilized community. Yeager, supra, at 369. The Ohio Supreme Court has made it clear that in order to state a claim for intentional infliction of emotional distress, the emotional distress alleged must be serious, that is, an emotional injury which is both severe and debilitating. Paugh v. Hanks (1983), 6 Ohio St.3d 72, 78. The Paugh court held that serious emotional distress may be found where a reasonable person, normally constituted, would be unable to cope adequately with the mental distress engendered by the circumstances of the case. Id. A non-exhaustive litany of some
17

examples of serious emotional distress should include traumatically induced neurosis, psychosis, chronic depression, or phobia. Id.
There is no evidence to support the Plaintiff-Appellant's claim that Young intentionally inflicted emotional distress on him as a result of her sending the Verification of Residency Form to the Lakes of Aurora. Plaintiff-Appellant claims that the suggestions from Young that Plaintiff-Appellant move out, or that there were loud noises as a result of other tenants using the door to Plaintiff-Appellant's building simply do not rise to the level of an intentional or reckless act on the part of Young. Moreover, Young telling the Plaintiff-Appellant that she would call the police if he did not stop harassing other tenants does not constitute intentional infliction of emotional distress.
Furthermore, the Plaintiff-Appellant has not indicated that he suffered any contemporaneous physical injury or that the actual emotional distress he alleges to have suffered was severe. In the instant case, the Plaintiff-Appellant has not produced any evidence establishing that Young's conduct was so extreme and outrageous as to go beyond all possible bounds of decency or that he actually suffered an injury. Simply stating that he was stressed does not constitute severe or serious emotional distress. There is no evidence that the Plaintiff-Appellant suffered an emotional injury that was severe and debilitating.
With respect to the alleged statements Plaintiff-Appellant claims that Young made to Penny Meschewshi, it should be noted that the Plaintiff-Appellant did not hear any of these statements. Therefore, there could have been no effect on him at the time they were made. Moreover, there is no evidence that he heard about these statements until after he
18

had initiated litigation against Young and Mayfield. Therefore, he has not produced any evidence that the alleged statements by Young had any impact on him prior to filing this lawsuit.
In short, Plaintiff-Appellant has not produced any evidence that Young intended to cause emotional distress or knew or should have known that anything she did or said would result in serious emotional distress to Plaintiff-Appellant. He has no evidence of a serious emotional distress injury and no average member of the community would find Young's conduct to be beyond all possible bounds of decency. Accordingly, the trial court properly granted summary judgment on Plaintiff-Appellant's claim of intentional infliction of emotional distress.
D. There Is No Evidence of Any Interference with Contractual Relations of Plaintiff-Appellant.
This tort was first recognized by the Ohio Supreme Court in Kenty v. Transamerica Premium Ins. (1995), 72 Ohio St.3d 415. At that time the Supreme Court held that the definition of this tort was as follows:
"One who intentionally and improperly interferes with the performance of a contract (except the contract to marry) between another and a third person by inducing or otherwise causing a third person not to perform the contract, is subject to liability to the other for the pecuniary loss resulting to the other from the failure to the third person to perform the contract."
Id. at 418-419.
19

has no demonstrated the requisite degree of fault necessary for Plaintiff-Appellant to make this claim. Moreover, as set forth earlier, Young was privileged to make the statements she did make in the context of filling out the verification of residency form and sending it to the Lakes of Aurora.
Plaintiff-Appellant's claim for tortious interference of a contractual relationship also fails given the lack of admissible evidence in the record. Furthermore, one of the elements of this tort is damages. Plaintiff-Appellant has not produced any evidence that he was damaged in his inability to obtain a lease at the Lakes of Aurora. He has not put forth any evidence that he has lost money as a result of having to live elsewhere nor has he pointed to any evidence of damages he had to incur as a result of failing to obtain an apartment at the Lakes of Aurora. If he indeed has paid more rent elsewhere, that evidence would be in the record. It is not.
E. Plaintiff-Appellant Has Not Established Any Breach of Lease
Plaintiff-Appellant mistakenly argues that his intent was to never pay for gas utilities, therefore, he cannot be required to do so. This ignores the plain language of the leases which he signed. A simple review of this language, found in the Utility Addendum Allocation, specifically provides that the rent does not include a charge for utilities. Instead, the resident paid utilities separately by way of a utility bill from AUM. Moreover, paragraph 11 of the Utility Addendum Allocation, the Plaintiff-Appellant agreed that, upon 30 days prior written notice from Mayfield, he would begin receiving a bill for additional
21

utilities and services, at which time such additional utilities and services shall for all purposes be included in the term "utilities" in the Utility Addendum Allocation.
Therefore, when Mayfield sent out a letter on November 1, 2005 indicating that they were going to start charging for natural gas as of December 1, 2005, they were in full compliance with the language of the Utility Addendum Allocation which was part of Plaintiff-Appellant's lease. By its clear language, there was no breach in the institution of a charge for natural gas under the Utility section of that lease.
Plaintiff's argument about the Utility Addendum Allocation language is misleading. As quoted by Plaintiff-Appellant in his brief, paragraph 11 of the Utility Addendum Allocation states as follows:
Resident agrees that resident may, upon thirty (3) days prior written notice from landlord to resident, begin receiving a bill for additional utilities and services, at which time such additional utilities and services shall for all purposes be included in the term "utility".
Based on this language, Plaintiff-Appellant argues that the use of the "may" means that this is a non-binding agreement. However, Plaintiff-Appellant is misreading this language. It is non-binding in the sense that the landlord will not automatically send a bill for additional utilities and services but may do so. Once that is done, "such additional utilities and services" shall for all purposes be included in the term utilities". [emphasis added]. Once the landlord does take the option of providing written notice and sending a bill for additional utilities and services, it then becomes mandatory, through the use of the word "shall", for that additional utility to be included in the term "utilities" in the lease. Plaintiff- Appellant's attempt to make this clear language ambiguous fails.

F. Plaintiff-Appellant Has Failed to Establish Any Deprivation of His Quiet Enjoyment of the Premises.
A covenant of quiet and peaceful enjoyment is breached when the landlord substantially interferes with the beneficial use of the premises by the tenant. Howard v. Simon (1984), 18 Ohio App.3d 14. The covenant is breached when the landlord obstructs, interferes with or takes away from the tenant, in a substantial degree, the beneficial use of the leasehold. Frankel v. Steman (1915), 92 Ohio St. 197, 200. The covenant of quiet enjoyment is implied into every lease contract for realty and protects the tenant's right for a peaceful and undisturbed enjoyment of his leasehold. Dworkin v. Paley (1994), 93 Ohio App.3d 383, 386. In order to constitute a breach of this covenant, the interference with a tenant's quiet enjoyment must be so substantial as to be tantamount to an eviction, actual or constructive. GMS Mgt. Co., Inc. v. Datillo, 2008 App. LEXIS 2626 at *26.
The evidence clearly demonstrates that the things complained of by Plaintiff- Appellant were minor and trivial. Moreover, he has not shown any actual eviction by Mayfield or Young nor has he even demonstrated constructive eviction. No reasonable person would conclude that the acts complained of by Plaintiff-Appellant were so substantial as to take away in a substantial degree the beneficial use of Plaintiff-Appellant's leasehold.

Assignment of Error No. 2
THE TRIAL COURT PROPERLY DENIED APPELLANT'S MOTION FOR ADDITIONAL DISCOVERY
Plaintiff-Appellant moved to compel access to Defendant-Appellee's property to take photographic evidence in order to present his case to the jury. This motion to compel was denied by the trial court after being opposed by Mayfield and Young. It was well within the trial court's discretion to deny this motion to compel. Plaintiff-Appellant had had plenty of time to request an inspection of Mayfield's property to take such photographs. By waiting until after discovery had ended, Plaintiff-Appellant has no clean hands to complain about the trial court enforcing its scheduling order.
The cases cited by Plaintiff-Appellant in his brief concern Rule 56(F) motions asking for additional discovery before a summary judgment motion is ruled upon. In the instant case, the Plaintiff-Appellant simply filed a motion to compel and the trial court denied it. At no time did the Plaintiff-Appellant file a Rule 56(F) motion asking for an extension of discovery to Mayfield and Young's summary judgment motion. The applicable standard is that a trial court has broad discretion when imposing discovery sanctions and a reviewing court shall review these rulings only for an abuse of discretion. Nakoff v. Fairview Gen. Hosp. (1996), 75 Ohio St.3d 254, syllabus.
At no time during the seven months of discovery after the case management conference, did Plaintiff-Appellant ever request access to Mayfield's premises to take photographs. In fact, as conceded by Plaintiff-Appellant, the first time this issue was raised was on June 12, 2008, ten days after discovery had ended. If photographs of Mayfield's
24

premises were so essential to the presentation of Plaintiff-Appellant's case, why didn't Plaintiff-Appellant make such a request during the seven months prior to the initial request. Furthermore, even if Plaintiff-Appellant took photographs of Mayfield's premises in August, 2008, they would not be admissible since they would not reflect the condition of the premises during the time the Plaintiff-Appellant resided there. Accordingly, they would be of no value to the jury in understanding the presentation of Plaintiff-Appellant's case, however he may have thought he could have used them.
Counsel for Mayfield and Young also objects to the characterization by Plaintiff- Appellant's counsel that Plaintiff-Appellant had been stonewalled by defense counsel. This insult has no basis in the record and can only be an intention of Plaintiff-Appellant to inflame this court. The depositions of Mr. Genberg & Ms. Lenese could have been taken at any time Plaintiff-Appellant subpoenaed them for deposition.
Finally, Plaintiff-Appellant's argument that he needed this photographic evidence to present his case clearly to the jury bears no relevance to the summary judgment proceedings. If the photographs were necessary for the jury, they were not necessary for the trial court to rule upon the summary judgment motion.
IV. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Defendant-Appellees respectfully submit that the trial court properly granted summary judgment to them and that the assignments of error cited by Plaintiff-Appellant do not merit an overturning of the trial court's rulings. The admissible evidence contained in the record and the applicable legal authorities clearly demonstrate that there are no genuine issues to any material fact and Defendant-Appellees
25

were entitled to judgment as a matter of law. Accordingly, Defendant-Appellees respectfully requests that this court affirm the rulings of the trial court and overrule Plaintiff-Appellant's appeal.
